# Exact simplex residual-vector compensation and the price of circuit drift
exact whole-body Brunn--Minkowski equality slice. They retain all
canonical simplex directions simultaneously and include arbitrary
integer tilts of those directions. They do not assert global
criticality, apply to arbitrary nonsimplex bodies, or prove OC.

The initial question was whether one shared endpoint translation
prevents the independent scalar losses in
`candidate 8426c7487ce19740`.
It does when the canonical circuit has zero total integer tilt. The
total tilt is an invariant that cannot be discarded for general
ambient caps. The exact correction below tracks it explicitly.

## 1. Normalization and the actual endpoint fractions

Let d>=1, m=d+1, and let T be a full-dimensional simplex of centroid
zero and volume V>0. Write its barycentric coordinates as

    lambda_i(x)=1/m+ell_i(x),       i=1,...,m.

The linear functionals ell_i sum to zero, and the map
`x -> (ell_1(x),...,ell_m(x))` is an isomorphism from R^d onto the
coordinate-sum-zero subspace of R^m. Let a,b>0 and delta in R^d, and put

    A=aT+delta,       D=bT-delta,
    K=(A+D)/2=((a+b)/2)T.

These are actual endpoint and midpoint sections of the convex body

    conv({-1}xA, {1}xD) subset R x R^d.

In particular the midpoint body attains whole-body BM exactly. This
normalization comes from translating the common midpoint centroid;
arbitrary initial endpoint translations v,w give
`delta=(v-w)/2` after that translation.

Consider all m canonical vertex caps of K through its centroid, with
arbitrary ambient integer tilts:

    H_i={ (z,x): ell_i(x)+beta_i z >= 0 }.

Let

    B=sum_i beta_i,
    q_i^A=1/m-ell_i(delta)/a+beta_i/a,
    q_i^D=1/m+ell_i(delta)/b-beta_i/b.                 (1)

The traces on the endpoint reference simplex T are respectively
`lambda_i>=q_i^A` and `lambda_i>=q_i^D`. Thus

    sum_i q_i^A=1+B/a,       sum_i q_i^D=1-B/b,
    a q_i^A+b q_i^D=(a+b)/m   for every i.            (2)

These are the shared constraints. Neither endpoint sum equals one
in general. In particular m unrelated ambient tilts cannot be
represented by a single translation unless their sum B is zero.

Define, for every real q,

    psi(q)=min(1,max(0,1-q)),
    phi(q)=(1-psi(q)^d)^(1/d).

The exact captured fractions and residual volume roots are

    p_i^A=psi(q_i^A)^d,     p_i^D=psi(q_i^D)^d,
    |A intersect (H_i)_(-1)|=a^d V p_i^A,
    |D intersect (H_i)_(1)|=b^d V p_i^D,
    |A outside (H_i)_(-1)|^(1/d)=a V^(1/d) phi(q_i^A),
    |D outside (H_i)_(1)|^(1/d)=b V^(1/d) phi(q_i^D). (3)

The same roots result from the closed opposite halfspaces. All these
boundaries have zero d-volume, but their nonemptiness is retained:

* q<0: the captured part is the whole simplex and the closed residual
  is EMPTY.
* q=0: the captured part is whole and the closed residual is its
  opposite facet, hence TANGENT and nonempty.
* 0<q<1: both parts have positive volume.
* q=1: the captured part is its vertex, hence TANGENT and nonempty;
  the residual is whole.
* q>1: the captured part is EMPTY and the residual is whole.

These formulas follow by taking the homothetic vertex cap when
0<=q<=1; its scale is 1-q. The extreme cases follow from the range
0<=lambda_i<=1 on T. The formulas are valid also when d=1, where
the tangent facet and vertex are endpoints.

Put

    r=d/m,       gamma=r^d,       kappa=(1-gamma)^(1/d),
    eta=m kappa-d,       c_d=(r/kappa)^(d-1).          (4)

The canonical source residual root, divided by V^(1/d), is
`kappa(a+b)/2`. Define the dimensionless root overshoot in direction i by

    Delta_i=[a phi(q_i^A)+b phi(q_i^D)
                -kappa(a+b)]/2.                     (5)

Actual volume-root overshoots are V^(1/d) times these quantities.
Here eta>=0 and c_d>0. For d=1, eta=0 and c_d=1. For d>=2,

    0<eta<1,        0<c_d<1.

Indeed `(1+1/d)^d>2` follows from its first three binomial terms,
so gamma<1/2, hence kappa>r. Also kappa<1. This proves all these
claims, without an asymptotic estimate.

## 2. An exact scalar-sum envelope

On the nonnegative half-line phi is nondecreasing and concave, with
phi(0)=0 and phi(q)=1 for q>=1. For d>=2 it is strictly concave
on (0,1). Explicitly, for 0<q<1,

    phi'(q)=(1-q)^(d-1) [1-(1-q)^d]^(1/d-1),
    phi''(q)=-(d-1)(1-q)^(d-2)
                    [1-(1-q)^d]^(1/d-2)<0.           (6)

The left derivative at 1 is zero for d>=2, so adjoining the constant
part preserves concavity. For d=1, phi(q)=min(q,1) on q>=0 and is
again concave. On q<=0 its value is zero; concavity is NOT asserted
across that endpoint.

**Envelope theorem.** For every real h,

    max { sum_(i=1)^m phi(q_i): q_i real, sum_i q_i=h }
       = E_d(h):=max{d, m phi(h/m)}.                  (7)

Both the maximum and the indicated attainments are genuine, even
though the constraint set is unbounded.

If every q_i is nonnegative, Jensen bounds the sum by
`m phi(h/m)`. If some q_i is negative, at most d terms are positive,
and each is at most one, giving the bound d. To attain d for any h,
choose d coordinates equal to a number L>=1 large enough that
`h-dL<0`, and set the last coordinate to h-dL. To attain the other
branch when it dominates, its argument must be nonnegative; take
every q_i=h/m. This proves (7), including existence.

The two branches meet at

    h_*=m(1-kappa)=1-eta.                            (8)

This follows from `phi(1-kappa)=r`. The envelope is d for h<=h_*,
and is `m phi(h/m)` for h>=h_*. It includes the eventual constant
value m when h>=m.

At h=1, define the exact nonnegative deficit

    J(q)=m kappa-sum_i phi(q_i),   sum_i q_i=1.        (9)

For d>=2, J(q)=0 precisely when all q_i=1/m. If every q_i>=0 this
is the strict Jensen equality case; if one is negative, the upper
bound d is strictly less than m kappa. A zero coordinate with all
the others nonnegative also gives strict Jensen inequality. For
d=1, in contrast, `phi(q)+phi(1-q)=1` for every real q, so J is
identically zero. This separates the boundary dimension exactly.

## 3. Zero total tilt: exact compensation across directions

Suppose B=0. Then both threshold vectors in (1) sum to one, so

    sum_i Delta_i = -[a J(q^A)+b J(q^D)]/2 <= 0.     (10)

This is an exact identity with two proved nonnegative terms. It
provides a compensation across the original directions even when
individual residual-root comparisons fail because an endpoint's
closed residual is empty. Equivalently,

    sum_i (-Delta_i)_+ >= sum_i (Delta_i)_+.

For d>=2 equality in (10) holds precisely when
`ell_i(delta)=beta_i` for every i. The two endpoint threshold vectors
then both equal (1/m,...,1/m). If all beta_i=0, this says delta=0.
For d=1 equality in (10) holds for every shared translation and every
zero-sum tilt vector, in agreement with exact cancellation between
the two opposite directions of an interval.

There is also a sharp bound on the total POSITIVE loss:

    sum_i (Delta_i)_+
       <= (d/2) [max(a,b)-kappa(a+b)]_+.             (11)

To prove this, when q_i^A,q_i^D>=0, concavity of phi and the weighted
coordinate identity (2) give

    a phi(q_i^A)+b phi(q_i^D)<=kappa(a+b).

Consequently a positive Delta_i requires a negative threshold in
one endpoint. Since kappa>=1/2, at most one of a,b exceeds
`kappa(a+b)`. Suppose this endpoint is b. A positive Delta_i must
then have `q_i^A<0`: if instead `q_i^D<0`, the sum of roots is at
most a<=kappa(a+b). In the positive case its value is at most
`[b-kappa(a+b)]/2`. At most d coordinates of q^A can be negative
because their sum is one. This proves (11); the other case is
symmetric, and if neither endpoint is large there is no positive
loss at all.

The bound is attained. Suppose `b>kappa(a+b)` and choose the
effective shifts `t_i=ell_i(delta)-beta_i` as

    t_1=...=t_d=b r,       t_m=-d b r.                (12)

They sum to zero and can be realized by one translation with
beta_i=0 because the ell-map is an isomorphism onto that subspace.
The endpoint residual-root vectors divided by V^(1/d) are exactly

    (0,...,0,a),       (b,...,b,0).

For the first d entries, `q_i^D=1` and `q_i^A<0`; for the last,
`q_m^D=1-d<=0` and `q_m^A>1`. The stated strict inequality for
q_m^A follows from `db>a`, implied by the dominance of b. In d=1
the last D-residual is tangent; in d>=2 it is empty. Thus d entries
attain the positive maximum and the last is negative. The symmetric
construction treats dominance of a. When the right side of (11) is
zero, zero is attained by zero effective translation.

This construction also displays the exact negative compensation:
the last loss is `[a-kappa(a+b)]/2`, and the sum in (10) becomes

    -[(m kappa-1)a+(m kappa-d)b]/2.

If C_A denotes the sum of the ACTUAL captured volumes from endpoint
A over all these directions, then the proof gives the additional
bound, in the case b dominates,

    sum_i (Delta_i)_+
       <= [b-kappa(a+b)]/2 * min{d, C_A/(a^d V)}.    (13)

Each positive-loss direction captures A completely, so its count
is at most `C_A/(a^d V)`. This normalized-volume bound is attained
together with (11) by (12), for which `C_A=d a^d V`. It is not a
bound tending to zero with the absolute volume of the smaller
endpoint; the scalar obstruction to such a bound remains valid.

## 4. Arbitrary total tilt: a sharp central regime

For any B, the two exact endpoint envelopes give the rigorous bound

    sum_i Delta_i <= [a E_d(1+B/a)+b E_d(1-B/b)
                         -m kappa(a+b)]/2.          (14)

This independent-envelope expression is not claimed to be sharp for
every B: endpoint optimizers must still satisfy the paired coordinate
identity in (2). That identity does, however, yield an exact joint
optimization throughout the interval

    -a eta <= B <= b eta.                            (15)

**Sharp central-regime theorem.** For fixed a,b,d and B in (15), the
maximum of `sum_i[a phi(q_i^A)+b phi(q_i^D)]`, subject to all the
constraints (2), is exactly

    m [a phi((1+B/a)/m)+b phi((1-B/b)/m)].            (16)

To prove it, (15) is precisely the condition that each endpoint sum
is at least h_* in (8). Each envelope in (14) therefore uses its
Jensen branch. The resulting upper bound is (16), and it is attained
simultaneously by taking each endpoint vector constant, with the
respective values displayed there. These constant vectors do satisfy
the paired identity. They are realized by delta=0 and
`beta_i=B/m` for every i, so the optimizer is an actual finite
canonical-cap construction.

For d>=2 the bound (16) is strictly smaller than `m kappa(a+b)`
when B!=0. In fact the weighted mean of its two phi arguments is
1/m. They are different for B!=0, both are positive in (15), and
the interval between them meets (0,1) in positive length. Strict
concavity on that interval proves the assertion even if the larger
argument exceeds 1. When B=0, (16) is exactly the zero-sum bound.
For d=1 the interval (15) consists only of zero, which is already
covered by Section 3.

## 5. A global explicit price for the total tilt

The tangent slope of phi at 1/m is exactly c_d from (4). Concavity
on the nonnegative half-line gives, for every real h,

    E_d(h)<=max{d, m kappa+c_d(h-1)}.                 (17)

For h>=0 this follows by applying the tangent bound to phi(h/m).
For h<0 the envelope is d, so (17) is automatic. Substituting (17)
in (14), and combining the two scalar maxima, proves

    sum_i Delta_i <= (c_d B-b eta)_+/2       if B>=0,
    sum_i Delta_i <= (c_d(-B)-a eta)_+/2     if B<=0. (18)

For example, when B>=0 the first endpoint contributes at most
`a m kappa+c_d B`, and the second at most
`b m kappa+max(-b eta,-c_d B)`. Their excess over the reference
sum is precisely `(c_d B-b eta)_+`. This proves (18) without
discarding an empty or tangent endpoint.

This bound is global and explicit, but is not asserted to be a sharp
joint optimization outside (15). In particular its zero-loss region
extends at least to

    -a eta/c_d <= B <= b eta/c_d.

It prices the original circuit's integer drift, not merely a chosen
translation of the endpoint bodies.

## 6. Why the drift cannot be removed

Under the common affine fiber shear `x'=x-u z`, the data change to

    delta'=delta+u,       beta_i'=beta_i+ell_i(u).

Their effective differences `ell_i(delta)-beta_i` and the sum B
remain unchanged, since `sum_i ell_i(u)=0`. Thus the preceding
arrays and all the bounds are invariant under this legitimate
change of coordinates. A nonzero B cannot be eliminated by a
common affine shear.

There are actual BM-equality examples with a positive loss in EVERY
canonical direction when B is unrestricted. Suppose
`b>kappa(a+b)`, take delta=0, and take

    beta_i=-b r for every i,       B=-db.

Then `q_i^D=1` and `q_i^A=1/m-br/a<0` for every i. Every left
endpoint is fully captured with EMPTY closed residual, and every
right captured part is a TANGENT vertex. Thus

    Delta_i=[b-kappa(a+b)]/2>0   for every i.

Replacing each beta_i by a slightly smaller value makes every right
captured part EMPTY and preserves the same residual roots. The
midpoint remains exactly `((a+b)/2)T`, and every cap is a canonical
centroid cap on that middle simplex. These are actual halfspaces of
the convex hull of the two lifted endpoint bodies. No global
criticality is asserted. This example proves that the restriction
B=0 in (10)--(13) is substantive, not a harmless normalization.

## 7. An intrinsic geometric expression for the drift price

The drift can be expressed without the arbitrary scale of the
reference simplex T or its defining linear functionals. Put

    U=|A|^(1/d)=a V^(1/d),
    W=|D|^(1/d)=b V^(1/d),
    B_hat=V^(1/d) B.

Then equations (2) give the intrinsic identities

    B_hat=U(sum_i q_i^A-1)
         =-W(sum_i q_i^D-1).                         (19)

For example, replacing T by cT changes a,b,beta_i by the factor 1/c
and V^(1/d) by c, so all three displayed quantities are unchanged.

There is a direct description from the actual cap planes. Let h_i(A)
be the altitude of simplex A from its ith vertex to the opposite
facet. Let s_i(A) be the signed distance of its centroid from the
ith original cap trace, positive on the captured side, with the
normal pointing toward that vertex. The barycentric gradient has
norm `1/h_i(A)`, and the centroid barycentric coordinate is 1/m.
Consequently

    q_i^A=1/m-s_i(A)/h_i(A),
    B_hat=-U sum_i s_i(A)/h_i(A).                    (20)

This identity holds for every actual trace, including planes missing
the endpoint body. It requires the true plane location, not a
projection of a plane back onto the simplex. An equivalent formula
using the right endpoint is

    B_hat=W sum_i s_i(D)/h_i(D).

The ratios in (20) are also invariant under any invertible affine
change of continuous coordinates, since the two distances in each
ratio are measured between parallel planes with the same transformed
normal. The overall volume-root factor transforms exactly like the
volume-root loss being bounded.

One can separate captured fractions and the support gaps that those
fractions alone fail to record. Let

    g_i^+=(q_i^A-1)_+,       g_i^-=(-q_i^A)_+.

The quantity g_i^+ is the distance from the vertex support plane to
an EMPTY captured halfspace, divided by h_i(A); it is zero when
the capture is tangent. Similarly g_i^- is the normalized support
gap to an EMPTY closed residual beyond the opposite facet, and is
zero when the residual is tangent. From (3), in every status,

    q_i^A=1-(p_i^A)^(1/d)+g_i^+-g_i^-.

Thus the exact intrinsic drift is

    B_hat=U [d-sum_i(p_i^A)^(1/d)
                    +sum_i g_i^+-sum_i g_i^-].       (21)

This is a proved expression involving actual cap fractions and actual
support gaps. Empty sections cannot be replaced by tangent ones in
(21): their equal zero volumes do not give equal g_i values.

Multiplying (18) by V^(1/d) now gives the wholly geometric form of
the price. If Delta_hat_i is the actual volume-root overshoot, then

    sum_i Delta_hat_i <= (c_d B_hat-eta W)_+/2
                                      when B_hat>=0,
    sum_i Delta_hat_i <= (c_d(-B_hat)-eta U)_+/2
                                      when B_hat<=0. (22)

The central regime likewise becomes `-eta U<=B_hat<=eta W`, and
its sharp bound is obtained from (16) by replacing a,b,B with U,W,
B_hat. Equations (19)--(22) provide a geometric interface for the
finite-vector theorem. They do not bound these support gaps for
globally critical caps or for an arbitrary lattice family.

## 8. Scope and relation to the earlier scalar frontier

The preceding statements use more than independently prescribed cap
fractions: the original canonical directions share the affine vector
relations (2). They give a proved compensation identity, a sharp
positive-loss bound, an exact central optimization, and a global
integer-drift bound on the simplex equality slice. Their empty and
tangent statuses come from actual endpoint sections, not abstract
zero-volume conventions.

They neither force the total drift of a genuine critical circuit to
vanish nor bound the corresponding drift across a general lattice
family. No claim is made that the simplex rigidity results elsewhere
force an arbitrary OC minimizer into this class. Those missing global
steps are not supplied by the finite-vector theorem.

passed 10,795 exact rational/interval checks in dimensions 1 through 12.
Its root intervals are certified by integer powers, with symbolic

the displayed formulas and cases; all general inequalities and
attainment claims are proved above independently of them.
